title: Karna's one dart
hookLine: Karna has one weapon he can use only once, saved for Arjuna, and in the middle of the night he has to decide
carry: dana: he gave even his armor

cards: Lamps. That's what the field looks like now.
The armies are so enraged after Jayadratha's death that they keep fighting into the night, and in Ganguli's telling, lamps are lit on chariots and elephants so the warriors can see one another.
Darkness belongs to someone on the Pandava side: Ghatotkacha, Bhima's son by Hidimba, a rakshasa, huge and powerful, and strongest at night. He tears into the Kaurava ranks, and they start to break.
Today, the weapon Karna has been saving, and who it finally hits.

teach.h: THE ARMOR, CUT AWAY AND GIVEN
teach.b: Karna carries a dart called the Shakti, and how he got it is the most well-known thing about him. Karna worshipped the sun, and he would not refuse a brahmana who asked him for something.
The god Indra came to him disguised as one and asked for the armor and earrings Karna was born with, the ones that kept him from harm. The sun had warned Karna in a dream.
He gave them anyway, cutting them from his own body.
In exchange, Indra gave him this weapon: it would kill any single enemy, but only once. Karna has kept it for Arjuna.
Now Ghatotkacha is tearing the Kauravas apart, and Duryodhana pleads: use it, or none of us will see morning. Karna throws.
Ghatotkacha falls, and as he dies, the text says, he makes his body enormous, crushing part of the Kaurava army beneath him. The Pandavas weep for Bhima's son. And Krishna rejoices.
The dart meant for Arjuna, he explains, is spent. The epic holds both, real grief and real relief. And look where it all began: with a gift.
Hindus still call Karna daanveer, the hero of giving.

teach.h: DANA: THE GIFT THAT SHAPES THE WAR
teach.b: Dana, giving, is one of the oldest duties in Hindu life, and the Gita calls the purest gift the one given simply because it should be given, to someone who can't repay you, at the right time and place.
Karna's gift cost him his armor; tonight it costs Ghatotkacha his life and keeps Arjuna alive. In this epic, a gift is never small.

how: Ghatotkacha is remembered in Hindu storytelling, and in some regional traditions, as Bhima's loyal son; his night battle and death are told in the Drona Parva of the Mahabharata.

o: Bhima's rakshasa son, who is strongest when the dark comes
the dart from Indra that Karna can throw only once

games.q: you're Karna. a brahmana asks for the armor you were born with, the thing that keeps you safe. the sun has warned you it's Indra in disguise. what do you do?
o: give it, because you do not refuse one who asks.
games.why: Karna cuts the armor from his body and gives it. Hindus still call him daanveer, the hero of giving, and that gift sets up tonight.

practice: Let your hands rest open on your lap, palms up, the way a gift is offered. Many Hindu families keep a habit of dana: a coin or a handful of grain set aside, food for a guest, a gift at the temple on festival days.

Breathing in, bring to mind one thing you could give this week to someone who can't pay you back. Breathing out, picture giving it with no strings. If you pray, offer it in your prayer; if not, let the intention settle.

wordCard.voice: Drona. His army fights on into the night, and Karna spends the one weapon he meant for Arjuna.

orig.note: Bhima's son by Hidimba, the rakshasa warrior of the night battle.

carryVoice: Your line: dana: he gave even his armor. One gift, long ago, and a dart spent in a single night. See you tomorrow.
